# github.com/coredhcp/coredhcp/plugins/searchdomains

Package searchdomains hands clients the DNS search list, the suffixes a resolver appends to a name that has no dot in it. It serves both families, and each one is configured on its own: a dual-stack server lists the plugin twice, once under server4 and once under server6, since the two configurations share nothing.

	server4:
	  plugins:
	    - searchdomains: example.org branch.example.org

	server6:
	  plugins:
	    - searchdomains: example.org branch.example.org

Every argument is one domain suffix, and they are searched in the order they are written. DHCPv4 clients get option 119 (RFC 3397), DHCPv6 clients option 24 (RFC 3646). Both hold the names as RFC 1035 labels.

## Nothing is validated

Setup never fails. There is no default and no check: whatever is written is encoded and served, including an empty list, which reaches the client as an option with no content. A typo therefore arrives at the client as a typo, and the place it shows up is a resolver appending a suffix that does not exist. A label longer than the 63 octets RFC 1035 allows is encoded with its true length in the length byte, which is outside the format; a client may reject the whole option over it.

## Placement

This is an option plugin. It never ends the chain and it never drops a request, so it belongs with the other option plugins: after server\_id and any filtering plugin, and before the plugin that hands out an address, because the first allocator to answer a client ends the chain. A plugin listed after this one that writes option 119 or option 24 wins, since each handler overwrites what the one before it left on the response.

## Behaviour

The option goes on every response the chain builds. That includes the ACK for a DHCPINFORM, which is the exchange a client uses to ask for options without taking a lease, and the response built for a DHCPv4 RELEASE or DECLINE, which the server throws away without sending.

Each response gets its own copy of the list. The encoder is handed a slice that nothing else holds, so a plugin further down the chain that edits the labels on the response cannot reach back into the configuration, and two handler goroutines never share one slice.
